section.title: The Unmarried and Widows
section.sectionRationale: Paul continues his reply about marriage by turning to the unmarried, the betrothed, and widows. In view of the present distress and the shortness of the time before Christ returns, he commends singleness as a way of undivided devotion to the Lord, while insisting that marriage is no sin. He frees the widow to remarry, but only in the Lord, and judges her happier if she remains as she is. The whole passage relativizes marriage and every earthly attachment under the passing away of this world and the nearness of Christ.
section.thesis: Because the time is short and this world is passing away, singleness is a good path of undivided devotion to the Lord and Paul commends it, yet marriage is no sin; the widow is free to remarry only in the Lord, though she is happier to remain as she is, for every earthly tie is now held loosely in light of Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the present distress and the freedom to marry without sin; the time is short and the world passing away; undivided devotion to the Lord; and the betrothed and the widow, free but happier as they are.

units.label: In view of the present distress

verses.text: Now about {{parthenos|virgins}}, I have no command from the Lord, but I give a judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy.
Because of the present {{ananke|crisis}}, I think it is good for a man to remain as he is.
Are you committed to a wife? Do not seek to be released. Are you free of commitment? Do not look for a wife.
But if you do marry, you have not sinned. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. But those who marry will face troubles in this life, and I want to spare you this.
What I am saying, brothers, is that the {{kairos|time}} is short. From now on those who have wives should live as if they had none;
those who weep, as if they did not; those who are joyful, as if they were not; those who make a purchase, as if they had nothing;
and those who use the things of this world, as if not dependent on them. For this world in its present form is passing away.
I want you to be free from concern. The unmarried man is concerned about the work of the Lord, how he can please the Lord.
But the married man is concerned about the affairs of this world, how he can please his wife,

and his interests are divided. The unmarried woman or virgin is concerned about the work of the Lord, how she can be holy in both body and spirit. But the married woman is concerned about the affairs of this world, how she can please her husband.
I am saying this for your own good, not to restrict you, but in order to promote proper decorum and {{aperispastos|undivided devotion}} to the Lord.

units.label: The betrothed and the widow
units.note: free, yet happier as they are

verses.text: However, if someone thinks he is acting inappropriately toward his betrothed, and if she is beyond her youth and they ought to marry, let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning; they should get married.
But the man who is firmly established in his heart and under no constraint, with control over his will and resolve in his heart not to marry the virgin, he will do well.
So then, he who marries the virgin does well, but he who does not marry her does even better.
A wife is {{deo|bound}} to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord.
In my judgment, however, she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

parthenos.gloss: A virgin, an unmarried young person. Paul addresses those who have never married, giving apostolic counsel rather than a direct command from the Lord, and commending the single life as a genuine and honorable option in view of the times.

ananke.gloss: Distress, necessity, hard pressure. The present crisis may refer to hardships already pressing on the Corinthian church, or more broadly to the tribulation of the whole age between Christ's comings. Either way it shapes Paul's counsel to hold marriage plans loosely.

kairos.gloss: An appointed time, a season, here the shortened time before the end. Paul says the time has been drawn together and is short, so that every earthly attachment, marriage, grief, joy, possessions, is to be held with an open hand in light of Christ's coming.

aperispastos.gloss: Without distraction, undividedly. The word pictures attention that is not pulled in many directions. Paul commends singleness not as superior holiness but as a life freed for undistracted, wholehearted attention to the Lord and His work.

deo.gloss: To bind, to tie. A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives; the marriage bond is for life. When death dissolves it, the widow is free to remarry, but Paul adds the crucial limit: only in the Lord, to one who belongs to Christ.

basic.context: Paul keeps answering the Corinthians' questions, now about those who have never married and about widows. He gives his considered counsel: given the hard pressures of the present time and the shortness of the age before Christ returns, staying single is a good choice because it frees a person for undistracted devotion to the Lord. But he is careful to say that marrying is not a sin. A widow is free to remarry, but only to someone who belongs to the Lord, though Paul thinks she will be happier if she stays single.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul flags that on this question he has no direct command from Jesus, so he offers trustworthy apostolic judgment led by the Spirit. His counsel is shaped by circumstances, the present distress and the short time, so it is wisdom for living, not a law binding every believer to singleness. Marriage and singleness are both honored; the deeper call is undivided devotion to Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul writes about the parthenos, the virgin or unmarried. His counsel is shaped by the present ananke, distress or pressure, and by the fact that the kairos, the appointed time, is short. He commends singleness as a life of aperispastos devotion, undistracted attention to the Lord. And he teaches that a wife is deo, bound, to her husband for life, freed to remarry only in the Lord when he dies.
basic.typology: The passing away of this world in its present form points forward to the new creation, when the shadow of marriage gives way to the reality it pictured, the marriage of the Lamb. Singleness lived for the Lord is a sign of that coming age, when believers neither marry nor are given in marriage but belong wholly to Christ.
basic.christ: Everything here is oriented to Christ: the shortness of the time is measured by His coming, undivided devotion is devotion to the Lord Jesus, and remarriage is to be only in the Lord. Singleness and marriage alike find their meaning in belonging to and pleasing Christ above every earthly tie.
basic.god: God gives some the gift of singleness and calls His people to hold this passing world loosely. He is worthy of undivided devotion, and He is honored whether one marries or remains single, so long as the heart is set on Him. Paul closes claiming the Spirit of God stands behind his counsel.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 19 records Jesus' words that some renounce marriage for the kingdom. Matthew 22 teaches that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage. Romans 13 urges holy living because the night is nearly over. 1 Corinthians 7 verse 7 already named singleness a gift.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible moves toward the marriage of Christ and His church, when this present world in its current form has passed away. Paul teaches the Corinthians to live now in light of that day: to marry or stay single as God gives grace, but in either case to hold this fading world loosely and give the Lord undivided devotion.

context.literary:
The passage is organised around a shift of voice that is easy to miss. It begins with the 'now about' that has been introducing the Corinthians' questions since 7:1, and with the same careful labelling of authority, 'I have no command from the Lord, but I give a judgment,' verse 25. Then the tone climbs. Verses 29 to 31 are the highest point of the chapter's rhetoric, five 'as if not' clauses stacked one on the other, and they are introduced by the announcement 'the time is short.' The rest of the section, verses 32 to 35, comes down from the height to explain what Paul means, and he says plainly that his aim is the Corinthians' freedom from concern.

There is a visible pattern in verses 32 to 34. Paul sets the unmarried man against the married man, and then the unmarried woman against the married woman, using the same two verbs in both pairs: each is 'concerned,' but the objects differ, the Lord's work or this world's affairs. Both sexes are addressed in equal terms, which was unusual in ancient writing about marriage.

The passage ends in two paired cases. Verses 36 to 38 deal with the betrothed, and each possibility is described in a balanced way: 'he is not sinning' if he marries, 'he will do well' if he does not, and 'does even better' for the latter. Verses 39 and 40 return to the widow, and the chapter ends where it began, with a statement of Paul's own judgment and an appeal to the Spirit. The closing 'I think that I too have the Spirit of God' is spoken with a touch of irony, since some Corinthians were claiming to be the spiritual ones.
context.historical:
Marriage in the first-century Greek and Roman world was usually arranged by families, and the 'virgins' of verse 25 were young women in the control of a father or guardian. A betrothal was a serious commitment, and a young couple could not simply decide for themselves. That is one reason verses 36 to 38 are hard to read, since the text speaks of a man deciding about 'his virgin' and one has to decide who he is.

Augustan legislation had pressed citizens to marry and to have children, and widows were expected to marry again within a limited time. A woman in the church who chose not to remarry was therefore going against social pressure. Paul's word to widows in verse 39 and verse 40 gives them freedom to marry and a blessing to remain as they are. Elsewhere he advises younger widows to marry, 1 Timothy 5:14, so his advice here is not a general ban but a response to the gifts and circumstances of each person.

The 'present crisis' of verse 26 is not identified. Some have pointed to food shortages in the Roman world in the middle of the first century, others to local pressure on a young church, and others to the general distress of living between the first and second comings of Christ. The BSB footnote gives 'impending' as an alternative, so Paul may mean something about to come. What is clear is that he expects hardship and wants to spare his readers.

The expectation that the Lord might return soon was part of the early church's atmosphere. Peter says the end of all things is near, 1 Peter 4:7, and Paul writes in Romans 13:11 that salvation is nearer than when they first believed. The 'as if not' sayings are an attempt to live every day as though the Lord might arrive before it ended.
context.canonical:
The strongest link is with Jesus' own words. In Matthew 19:11-12 He speaks of those who have renounced marriage because of the kingdom of heaven, in language that treats singleness as a gift given to some, and Luke 20:34-36 says that in the age to come people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Paul's counsel is an application of those sayings to the time between the ages. In Luke 14:20 a man excuses himself from the banquet because he has just married, and the story shows how easily good things can crowd out the call.

The Old Testament also knows celibacy as a sign. Jeremiah was told not to marry or have children in that place, Jeremiah 16:1-4, because judgment was coming, and his life became a message. Isaiah 56:3-5 promises eunuchs 'a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters,' a verse that shows that the lack of family was never final disgrace in the Lord's eyes. In the early church Philip's four unmarried daughters who prophesied, Acts 21:9, and Anna, the widow who never left the temple, Luke 2:36-37, show what undivided devotion could look like.

The call to live loosely to the world echoes Jesus' teaching on worry in Matthew 6:25-34, where the same Greek verb for being concerned is used, and Martha's distraction in Luke 10:40 shows the problem Paul has in mind. 1 John 2:17 says that the world is passing away along with its desires, and Romans 13:11-14 and 1 Peter 4:7 give the same urgency.

The widow's freedom to remarry in the Lord matches Romans 7:2-3, where a woman is released from the law of marriage when her husband dies. The picture of marriage that runs through the Bible ends in Revelation 19:7-9 and 21:2, where the church is the bride, so Paul's counsel is shaped by the fact that earthly marriage is a sign of a greater wedding.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants to relieve the Corinthians of anxiety and to give them a clear way of weighing choices. He is not trying to push anyone out of marriage or to rank the two states. He says plainly that marrying is no sin and that he is giving advice for their benefit, 'not to restrict you,' verse 35. What he wants is a church whose members, married or single, hold the world loosely and are free to serve the Lord without distraction.

He also wants them to see their circumstances through the shortness of the time. People tend to make decisions about marriage, grief, joy, money and possessions as if these things were permanent. Paul asks them to see each as passing. This is not an invitation to despise ordinary life but to put it in its place, so that nothing in it can master them.

Finally, he wants to honour the vulnerable. Virgins, betrothed women and widows had little power in that world. His careful balance, that each is free and each may choose, is a way of giving them dignity. He does not allow a father, fiancé or community to treat their choices as unimportant, and he insists that the widow's remarriage be 'in the Lord,' so that the Lord's claim on her is never lost.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Paul draws a clear line between what he commands and what he advises. 'I have no command from the Lord, but I give a judgment,' verse 25, tells readers that the preference for remaining unmarried is wisdom, not law. He repeats the point in verse 35, 'not to restrict you,' and verse 40, 'in my judgment.' Taking his counsel as a rule that all Christians should stay single would go beyond the text, and would contradict verses 28, 36 and 38, where marriage is clearly good.

The counsel is also shaped by a situation. The 'present crisis' and the shortness of the time are reasons given for the advice. People today who read the text rightly will not conclude that marriage is always more troublesome than singleness, but that they should weigh their own circumstances in light of the Lord's coming and of what he is asking of them.

Some things are prescriptive across time. Marriage is no sin. Undivided devotion to the Lord is the goal. A widow is free to remarry, but only in the Lord. And everyone is to hold the passing world with open hands. The 'as if not' sentences are not a command to be cold to a spouse, to avoid grief or to refuse to enjoy anything. They describe the inner freedom of someone who knows that these things, good as they are, will pass.

debates.question: Is the present distress a local crisis or the tribulation of the whole present age?

views.label: A specific hardship at Corinth
views.case: Paul may have in mind famine, persecution, or social upheaval pressing on the church, making marriage and family especially burdensome in that moment.

views.label: The eschatological pressure of the last days
views.case: Coupled with the time is short and the world is passing away, the distress may name the tribulation of the whole age between Christ's first and second coming.

debates.bearing: On either view Paul's counsel is wisdom for holding earthly ties loosely; it does not forbid marriage but reorients every attachment around Christ's coming.

debates.question: Who is the man of verses 36 to 38, and what is he deciding?

views.label: A man and his fiancee
views.case: The BSB and most recent translations read 'his betrothed.' The language of acting inappropriately and of 'she is beyond her youth' fits a couple who have been engaged for some time, and the phrase 'marry the virgin' reads naturally as a man marrying the woman to whom he is engaged. The BSB footnote notes the Greek is literally 'keep the virgin' or 'keep the betrothed.'

views.label: A father and his daughter
views.case: An older and widely held reading takes the man as a father who must decide whether to give his daughter in marriage. This suits the ancient custom in which a father arranged marriage, and the phrase 'give in marriage' appears in the Greek of verse 38. The father who holds back does so out of settled conviction and not out of compulsion.

views.label: A couple living together in celibacy
views.case: A third view, held by some in the early church, supposes a man and a woman living together as partners in a celibate union. Paul's concern would then be whether such a man, finding it hard, should marry her. Few modern scholars hold it because verses 25 to 35 give no hint of this arrangement.

debates.bearing: On every view the verdict is the same. Marriage is not a sin, abstaining is a good choice when it comes from a settled heart, and the decision should be made freely and not under pressure.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's counsel begins with epitage, 'command,' which he disclaims, and gnome, 'judgment' or considered opinion, which he offers. The same noun comes back in verse 40, 'in my judgment,' framing the whole section. Between the two he calls himself pistos, 'trustworthy,' and adds that this is 'by the Lord's mercy.' His trustworthiness is a gift, not an achievement.

The 'present crisis' of verse 26 has an unusual verb form behind it. The participle is enestosa, from a verb meaning to stand upon or to be present, and Paul uses it elsewhere for the things that are 'present,' contrasted with the things to come, 3:22. The BSB footnote offers 'impending,' which shows the translators weighed whether the crisis was already here or just about to be. Either way, it is pressing.

In verse 29 'short' is sunestalmenos, a perfect participle from systello, 'to draw together.' The verb is used of furling a sail and of wrapping a body, as in Acts 5:6, so the picture may be of time contracted or rolled up. The perfect tense says that the compression has already happened: the time has been shortened and remains so. 'From now on,' to loipon, marks the new situation.

The five 'as if not' phrases use hos me, 'as though not.' The last one in verse 31 is chromenoi ... hos me katachromenoi, 'using the world as not using it up.' The compound katachraomai is the verb Paul uses in 9:18, where he speaks of not 'using up' his rights in the gospel. The sentence is not telling believers to avoid the world. It tells them not to consume it or be consumed by it. The phrase 'in its present form' translates schema, the outward form or fashion, and the verb is present tense, paragei, 'is passing away.' The scene on stage is changing even as they watch.

Verses 32 to 34 turn on merimnao, to be concerned, anxious or careful, and amerimnos, 'free from concern.' Jesus uses the same verb in Matthew 6:25, 'do not worry,' so Paul's wish that they be without anxiety echoes the Sermon on the Mount. The unmarried person's concern is not worry but attention, and the married person's is attention given elsewhere. The word memeristai, 'divided,' in verse 34, is a perfect passive of merizo, to split or apportion.

In verse 35 Paul says he is not laying a brochos on them, a noose or lasso, the tool for catching an animal, and he wants euschemon, 'proper decorum,' good order and decency. The same adjective occurs in 12:23-24 for the parts of the body that are presentable. The goal is aperispastos devotion, a word built on the verb perispao, to be dragged about. Luke 10:40 uses that verb of Martha, who was 'distracted' by her serving. Paul wants a life that is not pulled in all directions.

Finally, in verse 39 the husband 'dies' is literally koimethe, 'falls asleep,' the Christian word for death, used again in 15:20 of those who have fallen asleep. The widow's freedom comes at a death that Paul has already described as a sleep.

typology.type: The passing form of the world, 1 John 2:17
typology.fulfillment: John says that 'the world is passing away, along with its desires,' while the one who does God's will remains forever. Paul's 'this world in its present form is passing away,' verse 31, uses an image from the theatre. The scenery of the present age is about to be changed. The correspondence rises when the new heaven and new earth appear, Revelation 21:1, and what passes is not creation itself but its present bondage. The type falls short in that the passing is not abolition but renewal, so the call to hold the world loosely is not a call to despise it.

The Lord told Jeremiah not to marry or have children in that place, because judgment was coming, and his life became a sign to his people. Paul's counsel to remain single in view of the present crisis is not a command but it has the same pattern: a life shaped by the nearness of a decisive day. The correspondence is fulfilled in Christ's own unmarried life and in those who follow Him for the kingdom, Matthew 19:12. It falls short in that Jeremiah's celibacy was a command, while Paul's is a gift given to some.

typology.type: The widow devoted to the Lord, Luke 2:36-37
typology.fulfillment: Anna was a widow of great age who 'never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying,' and she was among the first to recognise the infant Christ. She lives out what Paul describes as undivided devotion, verse 35. The correspondence is that a life set free from household concerns can become a life of prayer and recognition. The pattern rises in the church's later widows who served in prayer, 1 Timothy 5:5. It falls short in that Anna's freedom came from loss, not from choice, and Paul says the widow is also free to marry again.

typology.type: The marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7-9
typology.fulfillment: Earthly marriage is a sign of a wedding still to come. Revelation 19:7-9 announces that 'the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready,' and Revelation 21:2 pictures the holy city as a bride. Jesus said that in the age to come they 'will neither marry nor be given in marriage,' Luke 20:35. Paul's counsel puts these two truths together. Singleness for the Lord gives a glimpse of the age when all belong wholly to Christ, and marriage is the earlier picture of the union that will then be complete. The type falls short because the bride is not an individual but the whole people of God.

study.christ:
The passage is oriented to Christ by the clock. 'The time is short' only makes sense because of a coming, and in this letter the coming is the Lord's. Paul has already told the Corinthians that they eagerly wait for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, 1:7, and he will end the letter with the Aramaic prayer Maranatha, 16:22. The sayings about holding the world loosely are an expression of that expectation. A person who lives in the light of Christ's coming will not treat the best things of the present as ultimate.

It is oriented to Christ by the goal. Paul says that the unmarried person is concerned with 'the work of the Lord, how he can please the Lord,' verse 32. Pleasing the Lord is not one more duty beside others but the one thing for which the believer lives. The phrase 'undivided devotion to the Lord' in verse 35 describes the single-heartedness that Jesus praised in Mary, who sat at His feet while Martha was pulled in many directions, Luke 10:38-42. The Lord who deserves this devotion is not an abstraction but the person who gave Himself for His people.

It is oriented to Christ by example. Jesus was unmarried and lived in complete devotion to the Father's work, yet He honoured marriage by attending a wedding and by teaching its permanence. His life shows that singleness and marriage are both ways of honouring God, and that the real question is what a person is for. He also welcomed women among His followers, and the widow and the unmarried woman in Paul's account are included in His care.

It is oriented to Christ by the bride. Revelation 19:7-9 and Ephesians 5:25-27 describe the church as the bride of the Lamb, whom He loved, cleansed and will present to Himself as 'glorious,' holy and blameless. Every earthly marriage points to this, and every single person who lives for the Lord belongs to it. The single and the married in Corinth are both members of the same bride.

A caution protects the reading. Paul does not say that Christ requires singleness, nor that singleness is closer to Christ than marriage. He says that some are freed for a kind of service that others are not, and that all of them belong to Him. The widow who remarries 'in the Lord,' verse 39, is as much His as the one who remains as she is.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who is worthy of a whole life. The phrase 'undivided devotion to the Lord' presumes that He is able to receive and deserve all that a person can give. The question is not whether to love God a little and other things a lot, but whether any good thing is allowed to become a rival. A God who asks for undivided attention is not jealous in a petty way but in the way that suits one who is truly the best.

It shows a God who gives gifts and honours choices. The verses on the betrothed man and the widow stress freedom: 'let him do as he wishes,' 'he is not sinning,' 'she is free to marry anyone she wishes.' The God of the Bible does not manipulate His people into their callings by guilt. He gives gifts, 7:7, and then allows them to be received with joy. The only limit is 'in the Lord,' which is not a restriction on love but a protection of the covenant that has made the believer His own.

It shows a God who is Lord of time. The kairos is short because He has set it so, and the form of the world is passing because He is bringing it to an end. Paul's counsel is anchored in the conviction that history is moving to a goal that God has chosen, so the believer need not panic about the present crisis nor cling to the present order. God is not surprised by the hardships that Paul foresees, and He has not left His people to bear them alone.

It shows a God who cares about anxiety. 'I want you to be free from concern,' verse 32, is the wish of an apostle who has taken in the Lord's own words, 'do not worry,' Matthew 6:25. The God who commands trust is also the one who gives the reasons for it: His care, His nearness and His coming. He does not ask people to be indifferent. He asks them to put their cares in the right hands.

It shows a God who stands behind apostolic counsel without turning it into law. Paul closes with the claim that he too has the Spirit of God, and the sentence is a quiet reminder that wisdom that comes from the Spirit can be offered as counsel and still be weighty.

In worship this leads us to praise a God who gives both marriage and singleness, who is worthy of every heart, and who is bringing a world to its end in which every tear will be dried.

crossReferences.note: Jesus says that not everyone can accept the saying about staying unmarried, but only those to whom it has been given, and that some renounce marriage for the kingdom. This is the saying that stands behind Paul's counsel. He treats singleness as a gift, not as a rule or as a higher class.

Jesus says that those worthy of the age to come and the resurrection neither marry nor are given in marriage. It explains why Paul thinks of singleness for the Lord as a sign of the coming age and why marriage, though good, belongs to the present order that is passing away.

The Lord tells Jeremiah not to marry or have children in that place, because the coming disaster would fall on families. A prophet's unmarried life became a message about the days to come. It is the clearest Old Testament parallel to Paul's counsel in view of the present crisis.

The Lord promises eunuchs who hold fast to His covenant a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters. It shows that people without family were never outside His care, and it prepares for a church where singleness is honoured as a way of belonging to Him.

Martha is distracted by her many tasks while Mary sits at the Lord's feet, and Jesus says that Mary has chosen what is better. The verb for Martha's distraction is the root behind the 'undivided devotion' of verse 35. The scene is the best picture of the attention Paul hopes the unmarried will give.

Jesus says, 'do not worry about your life,' using the verb Paul uses for the concerns of the married and unmarried. The link shows that Paul's wish that the Corinthians be free from concern is an echo of the Sermon on the Mount and not a private anxiety of his own.

The world is passing away, along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God remains forever. John says what Paul says in verse 31. The passing of the present order is the reason to hold its goods loosely and to put the will of God first.

Paul tells the Romans that salvation is nearer than when they first believed and that the night is far gone. The same urgency lies behind the shortness of the time. Both passages turn the nearness of the Lord's coming into a call to holy living.

A married woman is bound to her husband as long as he lives, but if he dies she is free to marry another. Paul uses this as an illustration in Romans, and in 1 Corinthians 7:39 he applies it directly, adding the one condition, that she marry in the Lord.

Paul advises younger widows to marry, bear children and manage their homes, so as to give the enemy no opportunity. It shows that his word in 1 Corinthians 7:40 is not a general policy against remarriage but a judgment about the situation of those who are able to remain single.

Anna the prophetess, widowed for most of her life, never left the temple but worshipped night and day with fasting and prayer. She stands in the Gospels as a picture of the undivided devotion that Paul commends, and she is a reminder that widowhood can become a calling.

The marriage of the Lamb has come and His bride has made herself ready. It shows the goal toward which every marriage and every single life is moving. The wedding that earthly marriage foreshadows is the union of Christ and His people, and Paul's counsel is shaped by looking toward it.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with a man alone, a woman made from him, and a garden in which God walked with them, Genesis 2:18-25. Marriage is part of creation and is called good. At the same time, the story from the beginning points beyond the first marriage. The man and woman are placed under God, in His presence, and the happiness of their union depends on the one who gave them to each other.

After the fall, marriage continues, but it carries the marks of the curse, and it is joined with the promise that an offspring will come, Genesis 3:15. Much of the Old Testament is concerned with families and their continuation, because the promise runs through a line. In that setting, the lack of children was a sorrow, and singleness was rare. Jeremiah's unmarried life and the promise to the eunuchs in Isaiah 56 show that God was already preparing His people to see that the line of promise did not depend on the number of descendants.

With the coming of Christ, the promised offspring has come, and the line has reached its goal. That is why Paul can say that the time is short. The decisive event has happened, the Spirit has been given, and the ages are overlapping. In this overlap, marriage is still good and still part of the present order, but a new thing has appeared: people who give themselves to the Lord's work without a family of their own, and who are not lesser for that. The church is a family not formed by birth but by adoption, and its members are brothers and sisters in the Lord.

The passage also looks ahead. The world in its present form is passing away, and Revelation 21:1 shows what follows: a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city as a bride. Marriage is a sign pointing to that city, and singleness is a sign of the age when all are united to Christ. In the new creation there will be no more death, and nothing of what the faithful have given up will be lost, Revelation 21:4.

Until then, Paul asks the Corinthians to live as those between the times, free from anxiety, honouring both callings and keeping their eyes on the Lord who is coming.

quiz.q: What kind of authority does Paul claim for his counsel about virgins?

options.text: Trustworthy apostolic judgment led by the Spirit, not a direct command from the Lord.
options.note: Verse 25 says he has no command from the Lord but gives a trustworthy judgment.

options.text: A binding command from Jesus that all must obey.
options.note: Paul explicitly says he has no command from the Lord on this.

options.text: Mere personal opinion with no spiritual weight.
options.note: He claims to be trustworthy by the Lord's mercy and to have the Spirit of God.

options.text: A rule drawn only from Corinthian custom.
options.note: His counsel is shaped by the times, but it is Spirit-led apostolic judgment, not local custom.

quiz.q: Does Paul teach that it is sinful to marry?

options.text: No; if you marry you have not sinned, though married life brings added troubles.
options.note: Verse 28 plainly states that marrying is not a sin.

options.text: Yes; marriage is a lower, sinful compromise.
options.note: Paul directly denies this: you have not sinned.

options.text: Only for widows is remarriage sinful.
options.note: The widow is free to remarry in the Lord; it is not called sin.

options.text: Marrying is sinful only during a crisis.
options.note: The crisis makes marriage harder, but Paul still says marrying is no sin.

quiz.q: Why does Paul commend the single life in this passage?

options.text: It frees a person for undivided, undistracted devotion to the Lord.
options.note: Verses 32 to 35 present singleness as a life of undivided devotion to Christ.

options.text: Because marriage is impure and defiling.
options.note: Paul never calls marriage impure; he calls it no sin.

options.text: Because single people are holier than married people.
options.note: The point is undivided attention, not superior holiness.

options.text: Because the church forbids marriage.
options.note: No such ban exists; Paul upholds the freedom to marry.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean that the time is short and the world is passing away?

options.text: Every earthly attachment is to be held loosely in light of Christ's coming.
options.note: Verses 29 to 31 relativize marriage, grief, joy, and possessions under the passing world.

options.text: Believers should abandon all responsibilities immediately.
options.note: Paul does not urge neglect; he urges holding this world with an open hand.

options.text: The physical world is evil and should be despised.
options.note: Paul does not call the world evil, but passing in its present form.

options.text: Nothing we do now has any value.
options.note: The opposite; how we live now matters greatly in view of the coming age.

quiz.q: What limit does Paul place on a widow's freedom to remarry?

options.text: She may remarry, but only to someone who belongs to the Lord.
options.note: Verse 39 frees her to remarry only in the Lord.

options.text: She may never remarry under any circumstances.
options.note: Paul says she is free to remarry when her husband dies.

options.text: She may marry anyone at all with no restriction.
options.note: There is a restriction: the man must belong to the Lord.

options.text: She must remarry as quickly as possible.
options.note: Paul judges she is happier if she remains as she is.

questions: Paul commends singleness as freedom for undivided devotion to the Lord. If you are single, how might you embrace this season as an opportunity rather than only a lack?
The time is short and this world is passing away. Which earthly attachment are you gripping too tightly, and what would it look like to hold it with an open hand?
Paul wants believers to have undivided devotion to the Lord. What in your life most divides your attention from Christ, and how might you simplify?
Marriage is no sin, and singleness is a gift; both are honored. How can you resist quietly ranking one above the other, in your own heart or toward others?
A widow is free to remarry only in the Lord. How does the principle of belonging to the Lord shape the relationships and commitments you pursue?

translationNotes.note: The present crisis renders a word for distress or hard pressure; it may point to a specific hardship at Corinth or to the tribulation of the whole present age, and it shapes Paul's counsel to hold marriage plans loosely.

The BSB renders this of a man and his betrothed; an older tradition read it of a father and his unmarried daughter. Either way, to marry is good and no sin, and to refrain, where one is free, is also good.
She is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord, restricts remarriage to a fellow believer, only in the Lord, not to just any partner.
